title: Feedback on your argument
summary: You take a clear position and support it with what Sebastián's parents taught him. You can strengthen your argument by explaining why that family value outweighs the pressure Sebastián feels to pass.
overview:
We reviewed your argument with a simplified version of the Toulmin model, which looks at four parts:

- **Claim**: the position you take on the question.
- **Evidence**: the facts of the case you rely on.
- **Warrant**: the reasoning that links those facts to your position.
- **Qualifier**: how certain you are of your claim.

Open each criterion to see what it means and how it was evaluated. You can use this feedback to improve your argument.

items.label: Claim
items.description:
Your **claim** is your answer to the question: whether you are *in favor*, *against*, or have not yet taken a clear position.

This criterion only identifies your position. No position is worth more than another.

items.label: Evidence
items.description:
**Evidence** is the facts of the case you use to support your claim: what the people involved do or say, and the circumstances they act in.

It counts for more when you cite *specific* elements of the case, such as names, decisions or quotes, and for less when you only offer general ideas.

items.label: Warrant
items.description:
The **warrant** is the reasoning that explains why your evidence supports your claim. It is often left unstated; writing it out makes your argument easier to follow.

To find it, ask yourself which principle or value connects the facts you cite to your position.

items.label: Qualifier
items.description:
The **qualifier** shows how certain you are of your claim, through expressions such as *without a doubt*, *probably* or *in most cases*.

It can also come through in the tone of your argument, even without those words.

sections.title: Suggestions
items: You cite a specific fact of the case: what Sebastián's parents told him about earning things.
Explain in your own words why taking an exam for someone else goes against that value.
Think about how someone who believes that helping a friend in trouble is right would answer you.

sections.title: Your argument
sections.text:
I think his friend should not take the exam for Sebastián, because his parents told him that in their family you earn things through effort.
If he does it, they would both be deceiving the university.
